title: GenAIT: Development and Validation of an Objective Generative AI Literacy Test for High School Students
abstract: There is growing international interest in generative AI (GenAI) literacy and its assessment among high school students, but objective assessment in this population remains underdeveloped. This article reports the iterative development and validation of the GenAI Literacy Test (GenAIT), an 18-item multiple-choice test measuring high school students' conceptual knowledge about GenAI, with content spanning technical, practical, and human-impact domains. Expert review of relevance, clarity, and comprehensiveness provided evidence of content validity. In a large-scale survey of 7432 Estonian high school students, we evaluated the psychometric functioning of the Estonian-language GenAIT using confirmatory factor analysis, classical test theory, and item response theory. Results supported approximate unidimensionality, broadly adequate reliability for group-level research (marginal reliability = .72, KR-20 = .69), and good fit of a three-parameter logistic model (RMSEA = .013, TLI = .987, CFI = .990, SRMSR = .021). Measurement precision was sufficient for the majority of students but varied substantially across the latent trait, with lower precision for lower scoring students. GenAIT is therefore more suitable for group-level research than high-stakes individual classification. title: The AI Fluency Imperative: Cognitive Tax, the Diamond Workforce, and the Case for Consequence-Based Learning
abstract: Generative and agentic AI are lowering the cost of producing knowledge work while leaving responsibility for its quality with people. This conceptual paper argues that the result is a cognitive tax, the effort of directing, verifying, and answering for synthetic output, and that the tax falls hardest where expertise is formed. Drawing on recent evidence on novice productivity, early-career employment, and managerial strain, it distinguishes three levels of capability: information literacy, AI literacy, and AI fluency. It defines fluency as a judgment-based capacity: setting boundaries for autonomous systems, calibrating human sign-off to consequence, auditing outputs adversarially, and deciding when AI should not be used. Because the entry-level roles in which such judgment was historically formed are contracting, the paper argues that AI fluency cannot be produced by adding AI content to existing courses. It proposes a two-stage developmental model: a foundation stage of deliberate cognitive friction in coursework, in which students attempt problems before consulting AI and are assessed on how they reconcile the two, followed by a consequence stage of clinical-model internships, client-based projects, and student venture teams. The paper closes with implications for assessment, curriculum, and partnerships, and with an agenda for research on measuring judgment.

title: The Impact of AI Literacy on Employee Career Resilience and Adaptability in the Workplace
abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is transforming the modern workplace by reshaping job roles, skill requirements, and career development opportunities. In this evolving environment, AI literacy has become an important competency that enables employees to understand, use, and adapt to AI-based technologies. This study examines the impact of AI literacy on employee career resilience and adaptability in the workplace. It focuses on how employees’ knowledge of AI may influence their confidence in managing career challenges, willingness to acquire new skills, and ability to respond to technological changes. The study also highlights the importance of continuous learning, digital competence, and organizational support in strengthening employees’ career preparedness. A secondary-data approach may be adopted by reviewing relevant academic journals, research articles, and industry reports. The study aims to contribute to human resource management by highlighting the significance of AI literacy in developing a resilient, adaptable, and future-ready workforce.

title: AI Literacy for Teachers: An Ethical Imperative
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly influencing lesson planning, learning support, assessment, and teachers’ professional work. These possibilities also create concerns involving accuracy, bias, privacy, transparency, academic integrity, inclusion, and overdependence on automated systems. This review discusses AI literacy as a professional and ethical competency for teachers. It uses a narrative review approach, drawing on selected scholarship on AI in education, AI literacy, and international guidance for teachers. The discussion is organised around the meaning of AI literacy, its pedagogical value, major ethical concerns, and implications for teacher education. The literature indicates that responsible AI use requires more than operational familiarity with digital tools: teachers need to understand the limits of AI outputs, check information against reliable sources, protect learners’ data, identify possible bias, and make context-sensitive decisions about when AI is appropriate. International guidance also emphasises human agency, ethics, AI foundations, AI pedagogy, and professional learning as connected dimensions of teacher competence. Accordingly, teacher education should combine practical experimentation with case-based ethical discussion, assessment redesign, privacy awareness, and continuing professional development. title: What Factors Shape the Responsible AI in Accounting and Auditing - Evidence from Japan
abstract: This study investigates the interrelationships among generative AI risk assessment, AI policies, AI governance, and adoption practices using survey data from CPAs and corporate accountants in Japan. The analysis on a total of 372 valid responses show that AI governance, AI risk awareness, and training programs emerge as critical for mitigating risks and maximizing efficiency gains. Inadequate AI governance can exacerbate risks. Future responsible AI practices should focus on the need for structured AI policies and enough training systems. This study provides actionable insights for policymakers and practitioners seeking to integrate generative AI into accounting and auditing responsibly.

title: AI-Enabled Digital Co-Founders and Solo Entrepreneurship in Emerging Economies
abstract: Entrepreneurship in emerging economies is rapidly evolving as artificial intelligence (AI) becomes integrated into early-stage venture creation. However, limited research has explored how AI-enabled “digital co-founders” reshape solo entrepreneurship in resource-constrained environments. This study, therefore, examined how agentic AI tools influence opportunity recognition, resource mobilisation, and survival prospects for solo entrepreneurs in emerging economies. A qualitative desktop research method was used, drawing on secondary data from academic literature, global development reports, and industry analyses published between 2020 and 2025. Findings revealed that AI-enabled digital co-founders reduce traditional entry barriers, enhance market analysis capabilities, and support rapid prototyping, enabling solo entrepreneurs to compensate for limited financial, human, and technical resources. However, the benefits are unevenly distributed due to digital inequities, low AI literacy, and infrastructure limitations. The study recommends targeted AI upskilling, affordable digital access, and supportive innovation policies to ensure inclusive, sustainable entrepreneurial growth.

title: A Socio-Technical Analysis of AI-Driven Legacy System Modernization in the Public Sector
abstract: Purpose: This paper examines the socio-technical limitations of using artificial intelligence (AI) to modernize legacy information systems in the public sector, where continuity of services, policy obligations, security, and public accountability shape technology decisions. Design/methodology/approach: The paper combines a review of literature on public-sector AI adoption and legacy-system modernization with an anonymous survey of more than 50 public-sector technology professionals. Participants represented technical, analytical, management, application-support, and project roles and a range of professional experience. Survey topics included AI benefits and risks, organizational readiness, security and privacy, governance, workforce challenges, and human oversight. Findings: Respondents recognized AI's potential to support modernization but raised concerns about citizen-data protection, compliance, trust in generated outputs, integration, workforce readiness, and accountability. The findings suggest that AI should augment, not replace, experienced professionals and established engineering controls. Survey responses also point to the importance of governance, training, secure environments, phased implementation, and human validation. title: Operationalizing AI Ethics in the Brazilian Public Sector: Practitioners' Perspectives on Sociotechnical Challenges
abstract: Background: Incorporating ethical principles into public-sector AI systems requires software engineering practices that address technical requirements, organizational responsibilities, and potential consequences for citizens. However, translating these principles into development and governance practices remains challenging. Aims: This study investigates practitioners' perspectives on the sociotechnical challenges of operationalizing AI ethics in the Brazilian public sector, examining their motivations, perceptions, and expectations. Method: We conducted an exploratory survey with 130 public-sector practitioners working in information systems, AI, and digital governance. The instrument included 15 five-point Likert items across three analytical dimensions (Motivation, Perception, and Expectation) and three open-ended questions. We analyzed quantitative responses using descriptive statistics, internal consistency estimates, and exploratory correlation and subgroup analyses, and thematically coded 119 open-ended responses. Results: Items concerning legal compliance, transparency, and reputational risk received higher mean ratings than those concerning management support and social responsibility discussions, with a difference of approximately 1.2 points. title: Unseen AI: what Europe's public sector buys, and what its procurement registers cannot show
abstract: Procurement registers record what the public sector buys, not whether it contains AI. This white paper measures, for the first time with a published error, how much AI the European public sector buys and how much of it no one sees. It reads TED and the national registers of Spain, Italy, France, Germany and the Netherlands (January 2024 to October 2026) with keywords in every EU language and with an open-weights embedding model (BAAI/bge-m3), and measures both against a random gold standard of 2,317 purchases reviewed under a written rule anchored in the AI Act. Keyword counts are wrong: only 36% to 79% of the purchases that mention AI are AI, and keywords miss 4% to 29% of the AI bought. AI bought by brand (licences of Claude, ChatGPT or Copilot) and AI built into other products are not named at all. Governance is rarely bought: in TED, 15 of 815 large AI purchases buy an impact assessment, an audit, compliance support or AI Act training. Most AI is bought small, below what TED sees. Health is the sharpest case, two years before the AI Act’s high-risk obligations apply. The report recommends a mandatory AI label on procurement notices, governance budgeted inside AI contracts and framework agreements, and published validation for every count of public AI. The purchases found, the review decisions and the random sample can be searched and downloaded in the Arquestra AI Procurement Observatory (https://arquestra.dev/assets/ai-observatory).

title: Rethinking AI governance for social work through the triple mandate
abstract: Abstract As artificial intelligence (AI) systems become increasingly integrated into social work practice, questions arise about how they should be evaluated, monitored, and held accountable. Current AI governance frameworks, developed primarily for the private and general public sector contexts, rest on presuppositions that are rarely made explicit: AI deployment is inherently desirable, risks can be decomposed and addressed sequentially, institutions have adequate capacity to implement governance requirements, and affected populations participate voluntarily, with the ability to decline or appeal. Social work’s distinctive conditions (i.e. involuntary client engagement, irreversible high-stakes decisions, relational practice, professional discretion, and service to historically marginalized populations) create a context in which standard AI governance approaches fall short of securing accountability. Rather than proposing a new governance framework, this paper works diagnostically. We surface the conditions that current AI governance frameworks presuppose; trace how their failure in social work compromises transparency, contestability, and redress; and draw on Staub-Bernasconi’s triple mandate to propose a set of guiding questions for what any governance approach must address to remain accountable in this context.
authors: Eunhye Ahn, Moon Choi, Claire R. McNellan, Lauri Goldkind
venue: The British Journal of Social Work

title: From Regulation to Engineering: Organizational Privacy Climate as Mediator
abstract: Data protection legislation aims to protect privacy rights by regulating how information systems store and process personal information. While such legislation defines legal obligations, translating regulatory requirements into engineering practice is far from straightforward. As new frameworks such as the EU AI Act emerge, understanding these mechanisms becomes increasingly relevant. To investigate them, we conducted an online survey of 156 U.S. information system developers, examining the role of organizational privacy climate in the association between developers' perceptions of the GDPR and their privacy engineering practices. Using structural equation modeling, we found that organizational privacy climate mediates the relation between developers' perceived GDPR importance and their privacy attitudes, which in turn are associated with their privacy engineering practices. The mediation chain - regulation, climate, attitudes, practices - complements the direct effect of regulation on practice, revealing the organizational and attitudinal pathway through which regulatory intent reaches engineering behavior. We discuss implications for the next generation of privacy and AI regulation.
authors: Oshrat Ayalon, Eran Toch, Irit Hadar, Michael Birnhack

title: TESSA: A Governance-Oriented Custom GPT for SME Guidance under the EU AI Act: Design, Implementation, and Evaluation
abstract: The increasing adoption of generative AI presents new opportunities while raising AI governance and regulatory challenges, particularly for small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) navigating the European Union Artificial Intelligence Act (EU AI Act). To support AI governance education, this study developed TESSA, a governance-oriented educational artifact within the OpenAI Custom GPT environment. Following a design science research approach, TESSA was evaluated against baseline ChatGPT using 100 benchmark scenarios through governance alignment assessment, human expert review, and consistency testing. Preliminary LLM-assisted assessment showed governance alignment rates of 90% for TESSA and 83% for baseline ChatGPT, while independent validation by an AI regulation law practitioner yielded 71% and 70%, respectively. Human expert review indicated that both systems provided generally strong governance guidance, while TESSA maintained high consistency across repeated executions. The findings suggest that governance-oriented grounding can support structured, practical, and stable AI-assisted compliance guidance for SMEs. The study contributes (i) a governance-oriented Custom GPT artifact for AI governance education, (ii) a human-validated regulatory update mechanism, and (iii) a multidimensional evaluation framework for governance-oriented AI artifact.

title: Conflicted Records: Typed Adversarial Contracts for Auditable LLM Output Quality Enforcement
abstract: LLM-generated records increasingly populate production information systems where they are treated as data assets subject to the same quality expectations as records from operational databases. A single such record can simultaneously satisfy and violate a quality rule: a grounded fact adjacent to a hallucination, a useful answer adjacent to a stereotype. Classical data cleaning cannot resolve this because the two judgments are incompatible over the same span; a single LLM judge cannot either, since it shares the training biases that produced the conflict. Existing interventions such as prompt engineering, chain-of-thought, and RLHF reduce surface error rates but provide no audit trail and cannot distinguish genuine remediation from blanket suppression. The question is whether a deterministic check over structured inter-agent records can catch the defects that referential checks alone miss. We present BiasGuard-D: two adversarial roles drawn from distinct model families exchange typed claim documents, a three-model quorum adjudicates by majority vote, and a combined referential-plus-semantic invariant validates the verdict. The semantic component fires on verdicts referential checks miss; removing the iterative loop drops invariant satisfaction sharply. title: Prompting the archive: evaluating GenAI for primary source discovery in reference services
abstract: Purpose Primary source discovery is among the most demanding forms of reference work. This paper investigates whether generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools can find reliable and relevant primary sources, how effectively they summarize them and whether they can provide ethical access and enable discovery, to establish what reference librarians can responsibly recommend. Design/methodology/approach The authors tested four generative AI tools at free, institutionally provided and paid access levels, querying each with 20 prompts based on undergraduate history topics. A grading rubric framed by the Guidelines for Primary Source Literacy was used to assess primary source status, availability, summary, topic appropriateness and citation. Findings No tool hallucinated; all sources recommended by the tested generative AI tools existed. Overall, the tools performed well on topic appropriateness and adequately in citations, but some struggled to provide accessible sources and summaries. Research limitations/implications Because models evolve continuously and prior interactions may bias output, the study is not strictly reproducible, though the rubric and prompt set can be reused. Practical implications The findings support a reallocation of professional attention rather than a displacement of it. title: Bridging the Digital Divide Through Artificial Intelligence: An Inclusive Approach to Sustainable Education
abstract: The accelerating proliferation of digital technologies and artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming global education, yet it simultaneously threatens to entrench and widen existing educational inequalities. Historically conceptualized as disparities in hardware access, the digital divide has evolved into a multidimensional phenomenon encompassing connectivity access (first-order), technological and algorithmic literacy (second-order), and the capacity to translate digital competencies into socio-economic empowerment (third-order). This conceptual study executes an integrative literature review synthesizing peer-reviewed scholarship published between 2020 and 2026 across premier academic repositories, including Scopus, Web of Science, ERIC, IEEE Xplore, and Google Scholar. Guided by an inductive thematic synthesis approach, the paper critically examines the structural contradictions between rapid technological innovation and educational exclusion in underserved Global South and marginalized communities. The study proposes a comprehensive, five-pillar inclusive conceptual framework: equitable multi-tiered access, culturally contextualized adaptive learning, universal multimodal accessibility, decentralized cloud-edge infrastructure resilience, and ethical algorithmic governance. title: An experimental study on the mediating roles of career decision-making self-efficacy between digital media literacy and employment choices of university students
abstract: Algorithmic recommendation now shapes the career information university students see, yet whether raising students' understanding of these algorithms improves employment choices remains unclear. This study tested a dynamic bidirectional mediation model linking digital media literacy, career decision making self efficacy (CDMSE), and employment choices, with Algorithmic Awareness for Careers (AAC) specified as a distinct subdimension of digital media literacy. In a 2 × 2 factorial randomized controlled trial, 204 graduating undergraduates from three universities in southern China were assigned to Media Critical Literacy Training (MCLT), Career Algorithm Transparency Training (CATT), both, or neither; 192 completed four assessment waves ending 6 months after graduation. CATT mainly raised AAC (partial η 2 = 0.128), MCLT mainly raised critical literacy (partial η 2 = 0.096), and the two components jointly strengthened CDMSE. title: Is Your Data Ready for AI? What Five Years of Reports from 26 Regulators Reveal About Data and AI Governance
abstract: Working paper reporting, in brief, a document study of the 129 College Performance Measurement Framework (CPMF) reports filed by the 26 health regulatory colleges of Ontario, Canada, for 2020–2024. Each report was scored on a nine-dimension data and AI governance rubric, and all 1,030 forward-looking commitments were traced across the five reporting cycles. In brief: regulators report completing 56% of what they commit to and about one commitment in five is carried over unfinished; data quality is the least-described dimension; no report describes an AI impact assessment or monitoring of AI in use; and once data capability is taken into account, organizational size explains much less of which commitments get stuck. Detailed results are reserved for the full report. The codebook, scoring anchors, coded register and regulator-level results are not included. Findings are provisional. Conducted by Adelaide Advisory Group Inc., which provides consulting services to regulators.

title: Responsible AI at Scale_ Proposed Global Guidelines
abstract: Global issues need global solutions, and AI is one of them. These proposed guidelines give organisations that train, develop or use AI at scale one practical, voluntary baseline for every market. They draw on what the EU AI Act, the GDPR and the leading international frameworks have in common: the OECD AI Principles, the UNESCO Recommendation, the Council of Europe AI Convention, the G7 Hiroshima Code of Conduct, the NIST AI RMF and ISO/IEC 42001. The approach is risk-based and works through existing privacy, security and risk processes, without extra bureaucracy. It covers red lines, governance, training, deployment, AI agents, transparency, people’s rights, security, incidents and cross-border cooperation. Its practical tools include: control questions and suspension triggers that keep models and agents within their set scope a 90-day starting plan an integrated impact assessment a protocol for sharing incidents and lessons worked examples This record contains the full Guidelines and a two-page Essentials version. Version 1.0 of 18 October 2026, published for consultation. Regulatory references are current at that date. title: The Co-Production of Respect
abstract: The concluding chapter synthesizes the book’s central contention that respect is an expressive performance co-produced within the institutional context of urban education. Moving beyond traditional structural-based literature, the chapter employs Erving Goffman’s rituals of face-to-face interaction to analyze how educational inequality is reproduced through the contested meanings of respect. The research findings reveal that classroom conflict often stems from a reprisal process, which the author argues is a rational student reaction to feeling shamed or uncared for by teachers rather than an inherent oppositional attitude toward authority. By introducing the concepts of school cred and classroom capital, the author demonstrates how successful teachers maintain authority through reciprocal recognition and holistic engagement with students. Furthermore, the chapter proposes a broader theoretical framework of “doing inequality,” arguing that the proactive withholding of respect by those in power reinforces social boundaries across various institutional settings, including the medical and welfare fields. Ultimately, this chapter provides a roadmap for teachers to enact school reform, suggesting that understanding who is deemed “deserving” of respect is essential for reducing unequal power relations and fostering inclusive cultures in schools and society at large.

title: Popular planning: integrating co-production, insurgency and prefiguration in Latin American cities
abstract: Land conflict in urban and peri‑urban areas of Latin America’s large cities has intensified in recent decades, as market pressures and longstanding inequalities have exposed low-income communities to new instances of displacement and tenure insecurity. This paper examines community‑led responses to conflict in Rosario (Argentina), Santiago (Chile) and Belo Horizonte (Brazil), proposing ‘popular planning’ as an integrative lens. Popular planning refers to the coordinated practices that communities and supporting organizations use to engage with the state, which involve shifting logics of collaboration, confrontation and autonomy. A comparative analysis identifies three interrelated strategies – territorial, institutional and multiscalar – adopted by communities to defend place, influence policy and connect local struggles to broader networks. Across the three cases, these strategies are combined in different ways over time, deployed by communities to secure permanence and reshape planning outcomes. The paper advances popular planning as a framework for understanding how communities not only participate in urban development but actively plan it, contributing to debates in planning theory and Southern urbanism.

title: Scaling out while staying local: Maintaining inclusive co-production with vulnerable citizens
abstract: Organisations that involve vulnerable people in co-production face a paradox: while increasing the number of participants is seen as necessary to create greater social benefit, scaling risks undermining the locally rooted, relational practices that enable vulnerable people to participate. This paper develops a conceptual model that addresses this tension, by integrating insights from scaling of social innovation, collective action and group size, and scaffolding theory from the learning sciences. The model proposes representative co-producers and peer mentors as contingent, temporary scaffolding functions that support vulnerable people's involvement in co-production. At the same time, it argues that inclusive scaling requires federal group structures that maintain small-group interaction by coordinating multiple affiliated groups rather than enlarging single co-production arenas. The model offers a theoretically grounded framework for understanding how co-production with vulnerable people can scale without sacrificing inclusiveness. Points for practitioners: Scaling co-production with vulnerable people requires both differentiated support for participants and organisational structures that preserve small-group interaction as numbers grow. title: Co‐Production as State‐Building: Relational Capacity and the Prevention of Violent Extremism in the Global South
abstract: ABSTRACT This article advances a theory of co‐production as a relational state‐building strategy for countering youth radicalisation in fragile states. Grounded in fieldwork in northern Togo, affected by jihadist incursions from the Sahel and home to a predominantly young population, we argue that co‐production extends state presence into ‘brown areas’ and re‐legitimises authority by expanding the state's relational capacity to hear and respond to citizens. The framework specifies three interconnected mechanisms, face‐to‐face contact through service provision, civic inclusion via institutional channels, and the building of durable relational bonds, that jointly disrupt the recruitment pathways of extremist groups. Empirically, we show these mechanisms cultivate trust, dialogue and critical thinking among youth, while their structural reach is moderated by limited training and decision‐making authority. The findings reframe co‐production as a constitutive political force in state‐citizen relations, offering transferable insights for security policies across the Global South.
